analysis.one_liner: Makes sharing intimate images or AI deepfakes of someone without consent a federal crime and forces websites to remove them.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 20 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to knowingly publish intimate images of a person without their consent, including AI-generated "deepfakes," with prison time of up to two years for offenses against adults and three years against minors. It would also require websites that host user content to set up a removal process and take down flagged images within 48 hours, with the Federal Trade Commission enforcing the rule. The bill never received any committee action and expired when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of nonconsensual intimate imagery — disproportionately women and girls, and increasingly people targeted with AI deepfakes — would gain a federal criminal remedy, mandatory platform takedowns within 48 hours, court-ordered restitution, and forfeiture of offenders' proceeds. Anyone whose likeness could be faked or shared without consent, which is essentially everyone with an online presence, would gain a quick removal tool.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal crime of knowingly publishing a nonconsensual intimate image of an identifiable person — including AI deepfakes — punishable by up to 2 years in prison for offenses involving adults and up to 3 years involving minors, plus fines, forfeiture of proceeds, and restitution to the victim.

Requires covered platforms (websites and apps that primarily host user-generated content) to establish a notice-and-removal process and to remove a flagged nonconsensual image, and reasonable efforts to remove identical copies, within 48 hours of a valid request.

States explicitly that consenting to make an image, or sharing it privately with one person, is not consent to publish it — closing the argument that victims 'agreed' when the image was first created.

Makes violations enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission as an unfair or deceptive practice, so enforcement does not depend solely on prosecutors, and extends FTC jurisdiction to nonprofit organizations.
Makes it a crime to threaten to publish such an image for purposes of intimidation, coercion, extortion, or causing mental distress — the common 'sextortion' pattern.

analysis.who_pays: Social media platforms and other user-generated-content websites would bear the cost of building and staffing a 48-hour takedown system and face Federal Trade Commission enforcement if they fail. People who publish intimate images without consent would face criminal fines, prison, forfeiture, and restitution.

drawbacks.text: The removal process has no counter-notice: a platform must take down content within 48 hours based only on the requester's signed statement and good-faith belief, and the bill shields platforms from liability for good-faith removals 'regardless of whether the depiction is ultimately determined to be unlawful.' Someone whose lawful image is wrongly flagged has no stated process to contest the takedown, which invites over-removal of legal content.

The criminal offense for images of adults only applies where the person had a reasonable expectation of privacy, the image was not a matter of public concern, and publication was intended to cause or actually caused harm — a multi-part test that could leave some published intimate images without a federal criminal remedy.
Email services and broadband providers are excluded from the platform removal requirements, even though private messaging and email are common channels for sharing nonconsensual images.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a federal criminal prohibition and a fast takedown path for victims of image-based abuse, including AI deepfakes — is real and addresses a harm with few existing remedies. The cost is a takedown regime built almost entirely on the requester's say-so, with a 48-hour clock and no contest process, which courts and platforms would have had to work out and which risks sweeping up lawful content. A better-designed bill would pair the takedown mandate with due process for the accused poster; the benefit still outweighs the cost for a population of victims who currently have neither criminal protection nor a removal right at the federal level.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no markup, no vote, and no floor action, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Maria Elvira Salazar introduced the bill on July 10, 2024, with five original cosponsors from both parties — Madeleine Dean, August Pfluger, Stacey Plaskett, Vern Buchanan, and Debbie Dingell.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, which is the only action recorded in its history.
Twenty members cosponsored the bill by the end — 12 Republicans and 8 Democrats — but the committee never scheduled it for consideration.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and all bills not passed by both chambers died, including this one.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Platforms that would have faced mandatory 48-hour takedowns and FTC enforcement kept operating with no new federal removal obligation, and people who publish nonconsensual intimate images faced no new federal penalty from this bill. Victims gained nothing in this Congress, though a nearly identical measure passed and was signed into law in the next Congress in May 2025.

industries.industry: Social media and user-generated content platforms
industries.note: The bill would force any platform that primarily hosts user content to build a notice-and-removal system and remove flagged nonconsensual images within 48 hours, backed by FTC enforcement. Platforms avoided this compliance burden when the bill died.

The bill defines deepfakes to cover AI-generated or substantially modified intimate images and criminalizes knowingly publishing them; tools whose output ends up posted would feed a growing supply of criminal material. Publishing, not creation, is what the bill penalizes.

Many adult sites function as user-generated platforms and would fall under the 48-hour removal mandate and FTC jurisdiction, adding screening costs. Victims of nonconsensual uploads, a persistent problem on these sites, would gain a direct removal right.
